title: Puzzles: find the odd one, find the way, say why

summary.text: Four shapes sit in a row. Which one does not belong? You pick one. Someone else picks another. Can you both be right? You will test this with four cards, walk an ant through mazes, find what changed in a row and build a maze of your own. You will learn to say the reason for your answer, to go back to the last fork when a path stops, and to look in order. You will also find out which puzzles have one answer and which have many.
summary.art: A girl and her mother on a floor mat, each pointing at a different card in a row of four paper cards, both smiling.

intro.text: There are two good answers. The square does not belong, because the other three are circles. The blue circle does not belong, because the other three are red. Which one did you pick? Both are right, as long as you can say why. In this lesson you will find out when a puzzle has one answer, when it has many, and why the reason matters as much as the answer.
intro.art: Four paper shapes in a row on a floor: a red circle, a red square, a blue circle and a red circle.

outcomes: I can find the odd one out and say my reason.
I can find a second rule that makes a different one the odd one.
I can find the way through a maze and show its forks and dead ends.
I can go back to the last fork when I am stuck, or start from the end.
I can find what changed or where a piece goes by looking in order.
I can make a puzzle for someone and check their answer by its reason.

terms.meaning: A question you cannot answer straight away. You have to look, try and think.
terms.example: Which lid fits this dabba? You find out by trying.
terms.art: A child holding two steel lids over one round steel box, deciding which to try.

terms.meaning: The one thing you choose to look at when you compare things, such as colour, shape or size.
terms.example: With the rule 'colour', a blue circle is odd among red shapes.
terms.art: Four shapes in a row with a small label 'colour?' above them and the one blue shape circled.

terms.meaning: What you say after 'because'. It tells others why your answer is right, so that they can check it.
terms.example: The tumbler is the odd one, because the other three are food.
terms.art: A child pointing at a steel tumbler next to an idli, a dosa and a vada, with a speech bubble that starts 'because'.

terms.meaning: The one thing in a group that does not fit a rule the others fit.
terms.example: Crow, parrot, pigeon, cat. The cat is the odd one out, because the others are birds.
terms.art: Three birds on a wire and a cat sitting on the wall below them.

terms.meaning: Two things are the same in one way if they match in that way. If they do not match, they are different in that way.
terms.example: A red circle and a red square are the same in colour and different in shape.
terms.art: A red circle and a red square side by side, with a tick under the word colour and a cross under the word shape.

terms.meaning: A puzzle made of paths and walls. You must find a way from the start to the end.
terms.example: The ant must walk on the white squares to reach the banana.
terms.art: A small square maze drawn on paper with an ant at one corner and a banana at the other.

terms.meaning: The part of a maze you can walk on.
terms.example: In our mazes the white squares are the path and the black squares are walls.
terms.art: A line of white squares between black squares, with small footprints on the white ones.

terms.meaning: A place in a maze where the path splits, and you must choose which way to go.
terms.example: At the fork the ant can go down or go right.
terms.art: A path that splits into two, with an ant standing at the split looking both ways.

terms.meaning: A place where the path stops. You can only turn round.
terms.example: The ant walked down and met a wall on three sides. It was a dead end.
terms.art: A short path closed by walls on three sides, with an ant turning round.

terms.meaning: A winding path with no forks. There is only one way to go. Many people also use the word for any maze.
terms.example: A path that winds round and round to the middle, with nothing to choose.
terms.art: A round winding path drawn with one line that curls in to the centre.

explanations.context: This card says what a puzzle is. You have met three kinds in this lesson: odd one out, mazes and picture puzzles.
explanations.definition: A puzzle is a question you cannot answer straight away. You have to look, try and think.
explanations.description: A puzzle has a goal and it has rules. In a maze, the goal is to reach the end. The rule is that you stay on the path. In odd one out, the goal is to find the one that does not fit. Solving a puzzle is not like remembering a fact. You try something, see what happens and try again.
examples: Which lid fits this dabba?
Which way does the ant go to reach the banana?
What changed in the row while your eyes were shut?
explanations.art: A child sitting on the floor with a small paper maze, four shape cards and a pile of steel lids around her.

chart.title: A puzzle: which shape is hiding?

explanations.concept: Odd one out: find what three share
explanations.context: This card shows, step by step, how to find an odd one out. It uses an idli, a dosa, a vada and a tumbler.
explanations.definition: The odd one out is the one thing in a group that does not fit a rule the others fit.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. The things are an idli, a dosa, a vada and a tumbler. Step 1: look for something that three of them share. The idli, the dosa and the vada are all food. Step 2: check the fourth thing. A tumbler is not food. Step 3: say the answer with its reason. 'The tumbler is the odd one, because the other three are food.' The reason is part of the answer.
examples: Crow, parrot, pigeon, cat: the cat, because the others are birds.
Bus, auto, cycle, boat: the boat, because the others have wheels.
Three red circles and a red triangle: the triangle, because the others are circles.
explanations.art: A banana leaf with an idli, a dosa and a vada on it, and a steel tumbler standing beside the leaf.

chart.title: Three are circles. One is not.

explanations.concept: One set, more than one odd one
explanations.context: In the Odd One Out Test you looked for a rule for every card. This card says what you found.
explanations.definition: The same things can have different odd ones. It depends on the rule you choose.
explanations.description: Look at the row: a red circle, a red square, a blue circle and a red circle. Choose the rule 'shape'. Three are circles, so the square is the odd one. Now choose the rule 'colour'. Three are red, so the blue circle is the odd one. Both answers are right, because both reasons are true. An answer with a false reason is wrong. 'The square is odd because it is blue' is wrong, because the square is red.
examples: Banana, mango, lemon, carrot: the carrot grows under the ground. The lemon is the only sour one.
Crow, bus, mango, Moon: each one can be the odd one, with the right rule.
explanations.art: The same row of four shapes drawn twice, once with the square circled and the word 'shape', once with the blue circle circled and the word 'colour'.

chart.title: Same row, two rules, two odd ones

explanations.concept: A maze: forks and dead ends
explanations.context: This card names the parts of a maze. You walked through mazes like this one in Ant and Banana.
explanations.definition: A maze is a puzzle made of paths and walls. Some paths lead on. Some stop at a wall.
explanations.description: In the maze here, the ant walks on the white squares. The ant moves up, down, left or right, one square at a time. The ant does not jump over black squares. A fork is a place where the path splits and you must choose. A dead end is a place where the path stops. This maze has one fork and one dead end. Find them with your finger.
examples: A fork: at one square the ant can go down or go right.
A dead end: a white square with black squares on three sides.
explanations.art: A five by five square maze on paper with an ant at the top left corner, a banana at the bottom right corner and a child's finger on a fork.

chart.title: One fork, one dead end. Can you find them?

explanations.concept: Stuck? Go back to the last fork
explanations.context: This card shows, step by step, what to do when a maze path stops. You did this with beans in Ant and Banana.
explanations.definition: When a path stops, go back to the last place where you had a choice. Then take a way you have not tried.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. Step 1: the ant walks until the fork. Step 2: the ant tries one way, down. Step 3: the path stops. It is a dead end, marked with a cross here. Step 4: the ant goes back to the fork, not all the way to the start. Step 5: the ant takes the other way. The dead end was not a waste, because now the ant knows one way that does not work.
examples: Two ways at a fork, and one is a dead end: the other must be the way.
Looking for a lost chappal: each room you have checked is one room less to search.
explanations.art: A maze with a small cross drawn at a dead end and an arrow leading from the cross back to a fork, then on along the other path.

chart.title: The cross marks the dead end. Go back to the fork.

explanations.context: This card is about solving a maze backwards. You tried it on the mazes with three doors in Ant and Banana.
explanations.definition: You can solve a maze backwards. Start at the end and walk to the start.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. The ant can go in at door A, door C or door E. Only one door leads to the banana. You could try each door in turn. Or you can start at the banana and walk backwards. From the banana there is only one path, so you cannot go wrong. It brings you out at door A. In other mazes, going backwards meets the same forks as going forwards, so try both ends.
examples: Three doors and one banana: start at the banana and see which door you come out of.
Looking for a lost pencil: think back from the place where you last used it.
explanations.art: A child's finger starting on the banana in a maze with three doors and tracing the path backwards towards one of the doors.

chart.title: Start at the banana. Which door do you come out of?

explanations.context: This card shows, step by step, how to find a small change between two rows. You do this in the game Dice Switch.
explanations.definition: In a picture puzzle you find what changed, what is missing or where a piece fits. The trick is to look in order, not all at once.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. Two rows of shapes look the same, but one shape has changed. Step 1: put a finger on place 1 in both rows and compare. Step 2: move to place 2, then place 3, and so on. Step 3: stop where they do not match. Here it is place 4. The blue square has turned green. Looking at everything at once is quick, but it misses small changes.
examples: A cut-up picture: find the four corner pieces first, then the edges.
A missing thing on a plate: say each thing in order and listen for the gap.
explanations.art: Two rows of five paper shapes, one above the other, with a child's two fingers on the fourth place of each row.

chart.title: Check place by place. Place 4 has changed.

explanations.concept: A labyrinth: one path and no choices
explanations.context: This card is about a very old kind of path puzzle, the labyrinth. It is here because it is a maze with the choosing taken out.
explanations.definition: A labyrinth is a winding path with no forks. A maze has forks. In everyday talk, many people use both words for the same thing.
explanations.description: In a labyrinth you cannot get lost. There is only one way, and it winds on to the end. People have drawn labyrinths for a very long time. Coins from the island of Crete, more than 2,000 years old, show one. In India a winding path like this is often called a chakravyuha. That is the name of a battle formation in the Mahabharata. A stone carving at the Hoysaleswara temple in Halebidu, Karnataka, shows the young warrior Abhimanyu entering one. The temple is about 900 years old.
examples: The path here: 16 steps, and never a choice.
A queue that winds back and forth between ropes at a railway station.
explanations.art: A round stone carving of a path that winds in rings towards the centre, with tiny carved soldiers along it and one warrior at the entrance.

chart.title: A path with no forks

explanations.concept: The odd ones out in the night sky
explanations.context: Finding the odd one out is not only a game. This card tells how people found the planets by doing it.
explanations.definition: Long ago, people found the planets by noticing that a few lights in the sky did not behave like the rest.
explanations.description: On a clear, dark night you can see thousands of stars. Night after night, the stars keep the same places next to each other. But people long ago noticed five lights that did not. Week by week, these five moved among the stars. They were the odd ones out. The Greeks called them planetes, which means wanderers, and our word planet comes from that. The five are Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. They are not stars but worlds that go round the Sun, as our Earth does.
examples: A doctor looks for the one sign in your body that is not as usual.
A mechanic listens for the one sound in an engine that does not fit.
A farmer spots the one plant in a row whose leaves have turned yellow.
explanations.art: A night sky full of small white stars over a village roof, with one reddish light drawn a little larger and a dotted line showing where it was last week.

chart.title: The dark dots are stars. The red dot is Mars. Who moved?

explanations.concept: Other living beings solve puzzles too
explanations.context: People are not the only ones who solve puzzles. This card tells you about a slime mould and about honeybees.
explanations.definition: Many living beings find their way through mazes and tell what is the same from what is different.
explanations.description: A slime mould is a living being who looks like a patch of yellow jelly. Nobody has found a brain in a slime mould. In 2000, three scientists put a slime mould into a small maze, with food at both ends. At first the slime mould spread into every path, and then pulled back from the dead ends. In the end their body was one thin tube along the shortest way between the two meals. Honeybees can learn the rules 'same' and 'different'. In 2001, scientists trained bees to pick the colour that matched the one at the door of a small maze. The bees then kept to the rule with patterns they had never seen.
examples: A slime mould: every path first, then only the short way.
A honeybee: blue at the door, so choose blue inside.
Ants: a new line round a twig laid across their way.

perspectives.explanation: The slime mould and the bees are solving a puzzle. They try, they rule out what does not work, and they keep what does. That is the same thinking you used in the maze.
They say the slime mould is only growing towards food and shrinking where there is none. They would not call that solving a puzzle.

explanations.art: A small square maze in a dish seen from above, with a bright yellow branching thread running along the shortest path between two oat flakes.

chart.title: Two ways to the banana. A slime mould ends up on the short one.

agreed.text: The same four things can have more than one odd one out. It depends on the rule you choose.
agreed.evidence: In the Odd One Out Test, four cards gave four different odd ones: one by its dot, one by its shape, one by its colour and one by its size.

agreed.text: If you mark the paths you have tried and always go back to the last fork, you can get through a maze.
agreed.evidence: The French mathematician Édouard Lucas printed a marking rule like this in 1882. It came from an engineer named Trémaux. It works for every maze with clear paths, though not always by the shortest way.

agreed.text: A slime mould can find the short way through a small maze.
agreed.evidence: In 2000, Toshiyuki Nakagaki, Hiroyasu Yamada and Ágota Tóth put a slime mould in a maze with food at both ends. The slime mould left the dead ends and kept a tube along the shortest path.

agreed.text: Honeybees can learn the rules 'same' and 'different'.
agreed.evidence: In 2001, Martin Giurfa and four other scientists trained bees to choose the colour that matched a sample. The bees then did the same with stripe patterns they had never seen.

challenging.claim: Every puzzle has exactly one right answer.
challenging.context: This card looks at a claim that most puzzle books take for granted. It asks whether it is true of all puzzles.
challenging.for: In a maze, a path reaches the end or it does not. In a cut-up picture, each piece has one place. Nobody can choose a different answer.
challenging.against: In odd one out, the same four things can give four answers, each with a true reason. Books pick the answer most people see first. That is a habit people agreed on, not a law.

challenging.claim: Keep one hand on the wall and you will always get through a maze.
challenging.who: A very old tip, passed from walker to walker
challenging.context: This card tests a well-known maze tip. It matters, because a rule that works only sometimes can leave you stuck.
challenging.for: In a maze where every wall is joined to the outer wall, the tip works. Your hand leads you past every dead end and out again.
challenging.against: If the place you want stands inside its own block of walls, your hand never touches those walls. You walk round and round the outside. Marking the paths you have tried works where the hand tip fails.

challenging.claim: Puzzles are only play. They are not real maths.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that maths means sums, and puzzles are for holidays.
challenging.for: Puzzles are fun, and nobody needs to add or take away to walk through a maze.
challenging.against: In 1736 the mathematician Leonhard Euler solved a town puzzle about crossing seven bridges. His answer began a new part of maths about paths and joins. Looking for a rule, trying, and giving a reason is what mathematicians do all day.

big_questions.q: Can you make a set of four things with no odd one out at all?
big_questions.hint: What if two are red and two are blue? What if all four are exactly alike?

big_questions.q: Two people pick different odd ones, and both give true reasons. Is one answer better?
big_questions.hint: Is a reason about colour better than a reason about where the card is lying?

big_questions.q: Is a wrong turn in a maze a mistake?
big_questions.hint: What do you know after the wrong turn that you did not know before?

big_questions.q: Why do people make puzzles for each other, when the maker already knows the answer?
big_questions.hint: What does the maker enjoy? What does the solver enjoy?

big_questions.q: Does an ant know they are solving a puzzle?
big_questions.hint: How could you find out? What would you watch for?

big_questions.q: Is anything in the world odd in every way?
big_questions.hint: Think of the strangest thing you know. What does it still share with other things?

roots.context: We hunted for odd ones, walked through mazes and found changes. Now let us think about who decides the answer to a puzzle.

deep_truth.truth: In the Odd One Out Test, four cards lay on the floor. With one rule the square was the odd one. With another rule the blue circle was. You found a rule for every card. So no card is odd by itself: a card is odd only under a rule, and a person chooses the rule.
deep_truth.habit: We think every puzzle has one right answer, kept at the back of a book. But in odd one out, the cards do not hold the answer. The answer comes with the rule, and you have to say the rule.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Odd One Out Test, the same four cards gave four different odd ones, one for each rule: the dot, the shape, the colour and the size.

three.who_am_i: You are someone who can say 'because'. When you give your reason, other people can check your thinking.
three.what_is_life: A slime mould finds the short way through a maze. A honeybee learns to pick the one that is the same. Living beings of many kinds work things out.
three.what_is_this_world: The world does not come sorted. The night sky did not say which lights were odd. People looked, chose what to notice and found the planets.

roots.thread: Four cards on the floor are just four cards. Then you choose one thing to look at, such as colour. Now the cards fall into groups: three alike and one odd. Choose another thing, and they fall a different way. The cards did not change. All the different groupings come from one set of cards and one looker who chooses.

teachings.teaching: In this old Buddhist story, a king has an elephant shown to men who were born blind. One touches the ear and says an elephant is like a winnowing basket. Another touches the foot and says an elephant is like a post. Each is sure that the others are wrong, and they begin to fight.
teachings.link: Each man had a true reason, taken from the part he touched. In odd one out, each picker has a true reason too, taken from the one thing they chose to look at. The story adds a warning: your true reason does not make the other person wrong.

teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar says that whatever you hear, and whoever says it, wisdom is to find what is true in it.
teachings.link: A puzzle answer is right because its reason is true. It does not matter whether a child or a grown-up gave it, or whether the book agrees.

science.text: Honeybees can learn the rules 'same' and 'different' and use them on things they have never seen before (Giurfa and others, 2001). So telling what fits from what does not fit is not only a human skill.
Is the odd one out there in the things, or only in the mind of the one who looks? Thinkers still argue about this.

other_view.view: They say a good puzzle has one answer, and nobody chooses it. In a maze the walls decide. A path reaches the end or it does not, whatever anyone thinks. Even in odd one out, once the rule is said, the answer is fixed. Nobody can choose which card is blue.

practice.title: Three breaths at a dead end
practice.say: Think of a time you were stuck in a puzzle. Now sit still and put your hands in your lap. Breathe in slowly and breathe out slowly, three times. Do not try to solve anything. Now look at one thing in the room, such as a tumbler. Find three things about it that you never noticed before. Next time you are stuck, do the same. Stop, take three breaths and look again.
practice.kid: Sit still. Put your hands in your lap. Take three slow breaths. Now look at one thing near you. Find three new things about it.

ask: You and Amma pick different odd ones, and both give true reasons. Who is right?
Is a card odd when nobody is looking at it?
In a maze the walls stay where they are. What is left for you to choose?
Can a puzzle have no answer at all?

how_we_found_out.context: How can you be sure of getting through a maze you have never seen? This card tells the true story of an old tip that fails and a rule that does not.
how_we_found_out.story: People have built mazes of hedges and walls for hundreds of years. Walkers passed on one old tip: keep one hand on the wall and keep walking. In many mazes the tip works. But it fails when the place you want stands inside its own block of walls, not joined to the outer wall. Then the walker goes round and round and never arrives. In the 1800s a French telegraph engineer named Trémaux found a rule that does not fail. Here it is in simple words. Make a mark on every path as you enter it and as you leave it. At a dead end, turn back. At a fork, take a path with no mark if there is one. Never go down a path that already has two marks. The mathematician Édouard Lucas printed the rule in a book of maths games in Paris in 1882. A walker who follows it gets through any maze with clear paths, though not always by the shortest way.
how_we_found_out.who: Charles Pierre Trémaux, a telegraph engineer, and Édouard Lucas, who printed his rule
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Keep one hand on the wall and you will always reach the goal. This is wrong for a maze where the goal stands inside a separate block of walls. The walker circles the outside and never touches the walls round the goal.

story.title: A Pinch at Every Door
story.note: Kayal, Muthu, Valli akka and Paatti are made up. Chettinad, in Tamil Nadu, is a real region. Its old mansions really do have long rows of rooms round open courtyards. Rice flour is what many families use to draw the kolam at the door.
text: Paatti's house in Kanadukathan had more doors than Kayal could count.

It was an old Chettinad house, built by Paatti's grandfather. There was a front hall with tall wooden pillars. Behind it was a courtyard open to the sky. Round the courtyard ran a long verandah, and off the verandah opened room after room after room. Behind that was a second courtyard, with still more rooms. Most of them were kept shut. All the doors were the same dark wood, with the same brass rings.
Kayal was seven. Her cousin Muthu was five, and he was very good at hiding.
That morning the three cousins played hide and seek. Valli akka, who was eleven, found Kayal behind the grain bin in no time. Nobody found Muthu.
Then Paatti called them for lunch. Kayal came. Valli akka came. Muthu did not come.
"Muthu! The game is over! There is payasam!"
No answer. The house was very quiet.
"He has fallen asleep somewhere," said Paatti. "He does that. Go and find him, kannu, before his rice goes cold."

Kayal ran down the verandah. She pushed open a door. Sacks of rice. She pushed open the next one. Rolled-up mats. She ran across the courtyard and tried a door on the other side. Brass pots, stacked to the ceiling. She ran to the second courtyard, opened three doors there, and ran back.
She pushed open a door. Sacks of rice.
"I have been in here before," said Kayal.
She tried another. Brass pots, stacked to the ceiling.
"And here!"

She stood in the middle of the courtyard and turned round slowly. Every door looked like every other door. Which ones had she opened? Six? Ten? She did not know any more. She could run all afternoon like this, opening the same doors and missing the one that mattered.
Valli akka came out with a banana leaf in her hand. "Not found yet? I will look upstairs."
"Wait," said Kayal. She was looking at the front step. Beside it stood the little steel bowl of rice flour that Paatti used for the kolam every morning.
Kayal picked up the bowl.
She went to the first door on the verandah and opened it. Sacks of rice. No Muthu. She took a pinch of flour and dropped it on the doorstep, a small white heap on the dark stone.
"What are you doing?" asked Valli akka.
"Telling myself: not this one," said Kayal.
Next door. Mats. No Muthu. A pinch.
Next door. Old trunks. No Muthu. A pinch.

She did not run now. She went door by door, all the way round the first courtyard. Behind her, the white pinches made a dotted line. When she looked back, she could see at once which doors were finished.
"Eleven doors, and eleven times he was not there," said Valli akka. "That is a lot of wrong doors."
"They are not wrong," said Kayal. "Each one tells me where he is not. Look how few are left."
In the second courtyard there were nine doors. A pinch. A pinch. A pinch. Six were left. Then four. Then two.
Kayal stopped in front of the last two doors. Her heart was beating fast. If he was not behind the first, he had to be behind the second. There was nowhere else in the whole house.

She opened the first. Mattresses, piled high for the wedding guests who would come next month. On the top mattress, curled up like a kitten, with his thumb near his mouth, was Muthu. He was fast asleep.
"Found," whispered Kayal. She did not need the last door at all.
At lunch Muthu ate two helpings of payasam and was very pleased with himself. "Nobody found me for a hundred hours," he said.
Paatti came in from the verandah with her eyebrows up. "Who has been putting half a kolam at every door in my house?"
"That was me," said Kayal. "Every pinch is a place where Muthu was not."
Paatti looked at the long dotted line of white, all the way round both courtyards. Then she looked at Kayal.
"Leave them till evening," she said. "I want your grandfather to see how you looked for him."
story.epiphany: For the parent: Kayal fails while she opens doors in any order, because she cannot tell the tried doors from the untried ones. She succeeds when she marks every door she has ruled out. Each 'wrong' door then becomes useful: it makes the search smaller. At the end she knows the answer before she opens the last door. This is how a maze is solved: mark the dead ends, and never try the same way twice.
ask: Why did Kayal keep opening the same doors at first?
How did the pinches of rice flour help her?
Valli akka said the doors were wrong doors. Kayal said they were not. Who do you agree with?
When two doors were left, Kayal opened one and found Muthu. What if he had not been there?

experiments.title: The Odd One Out Test: can every card be the odd one?
experiments.context: In this test you lay out four cards and pick the odd one out. Then you ask other people, and you hunt for a rule that makes each of the four cards the odd one. The point is to find out whether a set has one odd one or many.
experiments.question: How many of four cards can be the odd one out, each with a true reason?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess: will everyone at home pick the same card? Then guess how many of the four cards can be the odd one: one, two or all four. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Everyone looks at the same four cards. Each person picks without hearing the others. A pick counts only if it comes with a reason, and the reason must be true for that card and for no other card.
