materials.item: paper for four cards, each about as big as your palm
a red crayon, a blue crayon and a pencil
a steel spoon, a steel tumbler, a banana or other fruit, and a pencil
three spoons that are exactly alike
a sheet of paper for the table

schedule.what: Pick the odd card and ask others. Hunt for a rule for each of the four cards. Do the same with four kitchen things. Then try a set of three spoons and a tumbler.

experiments.record: A table with one line for each card or thing, and the rule that makes it the odd one. Under the table, a grown-up writes what the child found, in the child's own words.

example_chart.title: What a finished table can look like (your rules will be your own)
cols: It is the only one that…

setup.art: Four palm-sized paper cards in a row on a floor mat: a big red circle with a black dot, a big red square, a big blue circle and a small red circle.
setup.caption: 1. Draw four cards and lay them in a row.

setup.art: A child pointing at one of the four cards while a grown-up writes on a sheet of paper, and a grandmother in the doorway waits for her turn.
setup.caption: 2. Each person picks the odd one and says why.

setup.art: The four cards with a pencil-written slip under each one: 'only dot', 'only square', 'only blue', 'only small'.
setup.caption: 3. Hunt for a rule that makes each card the odd one.

flow.do: 1. Tear a sheet of paper into four cards, each about as big as your palm. 2. Draw one shape on each card, as the table shows. 3. Lay the four cards in a row on the floor. 4. Say nothing about them yet.
flow.say: Here are four cards. Look at each one quietly for a moment.
flow.kid: A grown-up draws four cards. Lay them in a row. Look at each one.
flow.parent: Make the big shapes fill the card. Make the small circle about as big as a coin. Colour the shapes in fully, so that red and blue are easy to tell apart.

chart.title: The four cards
rows: a big red circle with a black dot in the middle

flow.context: This is the first step of the Odd One Out Test, a test where you hunt for a rule that makes each of four cards the odd one. Here you make the four cards.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child which card is the odd one out, and why. 2. Write the card and the reason in the table. 3. Ask whether everyone at home will pick the same card, and why. 4. Write that guess down too.
flow.say: Which card is the odd one out? Why? Will everyone at home pick the same card as you? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which card is the odd one out? Say why. Will everyone pick the same card? Guess, and say why.

ask.q: Why is that card the odd one?
good: It is the only square.
It is the only blue one.
It is the only small one.
It is the only one with a dot.

flow.parent: Any of the four cards is a good answer if the reason is true. Do not say so yet. Just write down what your child says.

chart.title: Your four cards look like this. Card A also has a dot, and card D is small.

flow.context: This is step 2 of the Odd One Out Test, a test where you hunt for a rule that makes each of four cards the odd one. Here you pick the odd card and guess what others will pick.

flow.do: 1. Ask one or two other people to pick the odd card, one at a time. 2. Each person must give a reason. 3. Pick a card yourself too, the one you really would pick. 4. Write every pick and reason in the table.
flow.say: Now let us ask the others. Each person must say which card, and why. Listen to each reason. Is it true?
flow.kid: Ask other people to pick the odd card. Each one must say why. Is each reason true?
flow.parent: If only two of you are at home, your own pick is enough. You can also phone a grandparent and describe the cards. If everybody picks the same card, that is a real result too. Go on to the next step.

chart.title: One family's picks (yours will be your own)

flow.context: This is step 3 of the Odd One Out Test, a test where you hunt for a rule that makes each of four cards the odd one. Here you ask other people to pick the odd card.

flow.do: 1. Ask how many of the four cards can be the odd one: one, two or all four. Ask why. 2. Write the guess. 3. Take the cards one at a time. For each card, your child hunts for a rule that makes it the odd one. 4. Write down each rule that is true for that card only.
flow.say: How many of these cards can be the odd one, each with a true reason? Guess first, and tell me why. Now let us test it. Start with card A. What is true about A and about no other card?
flow.kid: How many cards can be the odd one? Guess first. Then find a reason for each card. The reason must be true for that card only.

ask.q: What is true about this card and about no other card?
good: A is the only one with a dot.
B is the only square. B is the only one with corners.
C is the only blue one.
D is the only small one.

flow.parent: Give your child time. Card A is usually the last one found. If your child is stuck on A, hold A next to each other card in turn. Ask what A has that the other card lacks.

check.q: A big red square, a big blue circle and a small red circle lie in a row. Which rule makes the small circle the odd one?
check.why: Size. The other two are big and this one is small. Picking shape or colour means using a rule under which a different card is odd: the square by shape, the blue circle by colour.

chart.title: Fill this in for your four cards
cols: It is the only one that…

flow.context: This is step 4 of the Odd One Out Test, a test where you hunt for a rule that makes each of four cards the odd one. Here you test whether every card can be the odd one.

flow.do: 1. Clear the cards. Put out a steel spoon, a steel tumbler, a banana and a pencil. 2. Ask again how many of these can be the odd one. 3. Your child finds a reason for each thing. 4. Write the reasons in the table.
flow.say: Now four real things. Can each of these be the odd one too? Find a reason for each.
flow.kid: Now use a spoon, a tumbler, a banana and a pencil. Find a reason for each one to be odd.

ask.q: What makes this thing the odd one?
good: The banana is the only one you can eat.
The pencil is the only one made of wood. It is the only one that writes.
The tumbler is the only one that holds water.
The spoon is the only one you eat with.

flow.parent: Any fruit works in place of the banana. Check each reason together. Is it true for this thing, and false for the other three?

chart.title: Four kitchen things
cols: It is the only one that…

flow.context: This is step 5 of the Odd One Out Test, a test where you hunt for a rule that makes each of four cards the odd one. Here you try the same hunt with four real things.

flow.do: 1. Put out three spoons that are exactly alike, and one tumbler. 2. Ask which is the odd one. 3. Then ask your child to find a reason for one of the spoons to be the odd one. 4. Talk about why this is so hard.
flow.say: Three spoons and one tumbler. Which is the odd one? Now try to make one of the spoons the odd one. Can you?
flow.kid: Three spoons and one tumbler. Which is odd? Now try to make a spoon the odd one. Can you?

ask.q: Why is it so hard to make a spoon the odd one?
good: The spoons are all the same.
Anything I say about one spoon is true of the other spoons too.

flow.parent: Some children say 'this spoon is the one on the left'. That is clever. Mix the spoons up and ask whether the same spoon is still the odd one. A good rule is about the thing itself, not about where it lies.

chart.title: Three alike and one different

flow.context: This is step 6 of the Odd One Out Test, a test where you hunt for a rule that makes each of four cards the odd one. Here you try a set where three things are exactly alike.

flow.do: 1. Ask what your child found out. 2. Ask what they saw that makes them think so. 3. Write their words under the table. 4. Only then say it in one sentence: the rule decides which one is odd.
flow.say: What did you find out? What did you see that makes you think so? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you found out. Say what you saw. Say why you think so.

ask.q: How many of the four cards could be the odd one?
good: All four.
Every card, if I chose the right rule.
It depends on what you look at.

flow.parent: A strong answer sounds like this: 'I thought only one card was odd. But I found a reason for every card. It depends on the rule. With three spoons exactly alike, only the tumbler could be odd.'
flow.context: This is the last step of the Odd One Out Test, a test where you hunt for a rule that makes each of four cards the odd one. Here you say what you found.

activities.title: Ant and Banana: finding the way through a maze
activities.context: In this activity you help an ant reach a banana through four mazes. You mark the dead ends with chana and go back to the last fork. The point is to find out what to do when a path stops, and when it helps to start from the end.
activities.problem: A path in a maze stops at a wall. What is the best thing to do next?

materials.item: paper and a pencil
one rajma, to be the ant
chana or buttons, to mark dead ends

schedule.what: Trace a small maze with a finger. Walk a rajma through a big maze on paper and mark the dead ends. Then solve two mazes with three doors, starting from the banana.

activities.record: Keep the paper maze. Draw a small cross on every dead end you met, and draw your way from the ant to the banana with a crayon.

setup.art: A child's finger tracing along white squares of a small maze on a phone screen, from an ant in one corner towards a banana in the other.
setup.caption: 1. Trace the small maze with a finger.

setup.art: A six by six maze drawn in pencil on paper with the wall squares shaded, a rajma on the path and a chana sitting on a dead-end square.
setup.caption: 2. Walk a rajma through the big maze. Leave a chana at each dead end.

setup.art: A maze with three open doors at the top labelled A, C and E and a banana at the bottom, with a child's finger starting on the banana.
setup.caption: 3. Three doors: start at the banana and walk backwards.

flow.do: 1. Show the small maze on the screen. 2. Say the rules: walk on white squares only, one square at a time, up, down, left or right. 3. Your child traces the way to the banana with a finger. 4. Ask where the path split, and where it stopped.
flow.say: Help the ant reach the banana. Walk only on the white squares. No jumping over black squares, and no slanting steps.
flow.kid: Help the ant reach the banana. Walk on white squares only. Go up, down, left or right.

ask.q: Where did the path split into two?
good: Where I could go down or go right.
At the second square of the second row.

chart.title: The small maze

flow.context: This is the first step of Ant and Banana, where you find the way through mazes and learn what to do at a dead end. Here you trace a small maze with your finger.

flow.do: 1. Copy the big maze on paper, 6 squares by 6 squares, and shade the black squares. 2. Your child guesses which way to go at the first fork, and says why. 3. Your child moves a rajma along the path. 4. At each dead end, your child leaves a chana there and goes back to the last fork.
flow.say: Look at the big maze. Which way will you try at the first fork? Why? When the path stops, leave a chana there. Then go back to the last fork and try another way.
flow.kid: Move your rajma along the white squares. At a dead end, leave a chana. Go back to the last fork. Try another way.

ask.q: You left a chana at a dead end. What does that chana tell you?
good: Not this way.
I have tried here already.
The way must be one of the others.

flow.parent: Make each square about two fingers wide. Copying takes about three minutes, and you can do it while your child traces the small maze. This maze has two forks and two dead ends. Your child may meet both, one or none.

check.q: The ant's path stops at a wall. Where should the ant go back to?
check.why: The last fork. That is the nearest place with a way not yet tried. Picking the very start means walking again over squares that were fine.

chart.title: The big maze: copy this on paper

flow.context: This is step 2 of Ant and Banana, where you find the way through mazes and learn what to do at a dead end. Here you walk a rajma through a big maze and mark the dead ends.

flow.do: 1. Show the maze with three doors. The ant may go in at door A, C or E. 2. Your child guesses which door leads to the banana, and says why. 3. Your child tests the guess with a finger. 4. Then your child starts at the banana and traces backwards to a door.
flow.say: The ant can go in at A, C or E. Which door do you think is right? Why? Test it. Now start at the banana and walk backwards. Where do you come out?
flow.kid: Guess the right door: A, C or E. Test it. Then start at the banana. Walk backwards. Which door do you reach?

ask.q: Which was quicker: trying the doors, or starting from the banana? Why?
good: From the banana. There was only one path.
From the doors I had to try more than one.

flow.parent: From the banana there is only one path, with no fork, so your child cannot go wrong. Door C is the right one. Starting from the end is quick here, but it does not help in every maze.

chart.title: Three doors, one banana

flow.context: This is step 3 of Ant and Banana, where you find the way through mazes and learn what to do at a dead end. Here you solve a maze with three doors, forwards and then backwards.

flow.do: 1. Show the last maze. 2. Your child solves it in any way they like. 3. Ask what your child found out about dead ends and about starting from the end. 4. Listen first. Then say it in one sentence.
flow.say: One more maze. Solve it any way you like. Then tell me: what do you do at a dead end? When does it help to start at the end?
flow.kid: Solve the last maze your own way. Then say what you do at a dead end.

ask.q: What do you do when the path stops?
good: Go back to the last fork.
Try a way I have not tried.
Remember that way is no good.

flow.parent: After your child has answered, you can say it: a dead end tells you one way that does not work, so you go back to the last fork and try another.

check.q: In the last maze, which door leads the ant to the banana?
check.why: Door E. Start at the banana and walk backwards: the path goes up, right, right and then up to door E. Door A is a long path that stops at the bottom, one wall away from the banana. Door C stops after two squares.

chart.title: The last maze: which door?

flow.context: This is the last step of Ant and Banana, where you find the way through mazes and learn what to do at a dead end. Here you solve one more maze and say what you found.

activities.title: The Cut-Up Picture: where does each piece go?
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up cuts an old card into 4 pieces and then 8 pieces, and you put the picture together again. The point is to find out which pieces are best to place first, and how to tell what is missing.
activities.problem: A picture is in pieces. How do you work out where each piece goes without trying every place?

materials.item: an old greeting card, wedding invitation or the front of a biscuit carton, with a clear picture
a dark crayon or sketch pen
scissors, for the grown-up
an envelope to keep the pieces in

activities.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting.

schedule.what: Draw a border round a picture. Cut it into 4 pieces and put it together. Cut it into 8 pieces and put it together, corners first. Then find which piece is missing.

activities.record: Keep the pieces in an envelope. On the envelope, write how many pieces there are and which pieces you placed first.

setup.art: A child drawing a thick dark crayon border round the edge of a picture on an old greeting card.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a thick border round the picture.

setup.art: A grown-up cutting the card into four pieces with scissors, with the pieces falling on a mat.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up cuts it into 4 pieces, and later 8.

setup.art: A child fitting eight small card pieces together on the floor, with the four corner pieces already in place and the border showing on their outer sides.
setup.caption: 3. Put it together. Corners first.

flow.do: 1. Choose a card with a clear picture. 2. Your child draws a thick dark line all round the edge of the picture. 3. Ask your child to name five things in the picture. 4. On the back, draw one line across and one line down, to make 4 equal parts.
flow.say: Draw a thick border round the picture. Now look hard. Tell me five things you can see in it.
flow.kid: Draw a thick line round the edge of the picture. Name five things you see in it.
flow.parent: The border matters. Later it shows which pieces belong on the outside of the picture.

chart.title: One line across, one line down: 4 pieces

flow.context: This is the first step of the Cut-Up Picture, where a picture is cut into pieces and you put it together again. Here you look closely at the picture and draw a border round it.

flow.do: 1. Cut along the two lines to make 4 pieces. 2. Mix the pieces and turn some of them round. 3. Your child puts the picture together. 4. Ask how your child knew where each piece went.
flow.say: Here are four pieces, all mixed up. Put the picture together. How do you know where each piece goes?
flow.kid: Put the 4 pieces together. How do you know where each piece goes?

ask.q: How did you know where this piece goes?
good: The picture carries on from this piece to that one.
The border is on two sides, so it is a corner.
This piece shows the top of the tree, so I put the piece at the top.

flow.context: This is step 2 of the Cut-Up Picture, where a picture is cut into pieces and you put it together again. Here you put 4 pieces together.

flow.do: 1. Ask how many pieces there will be if each piece is cut in two. Ask whether it will be harder, and why. 2. Cut each piece in two, from top to bottom. 3. Mix the pieces. 4. Your child first finds the pieces with border on two sides, then puts the picture together.
flow.say: I will cut each piece in two. How many pieces will there be? Will the puzzle be harder? Why? Find the pieces with border on two sides first.
flow.kid: Each piece is cut in two. How many pieces now? Find the pieces with border on two sides first.

ask.q: Why is it a good idea to place the corner pieces first?
good: There are only four corners, so each corner piece has few places to go.
The border shows me which way round it goes.

flow.parent: There are now 8 pieces in 2 rows of 4. Four of them are corner pieces, with border on two sides. The other four have border on one side only.

check.q: A piece of a cut-up picture has border along two sides that meet. Where does it go?
check.why: In a corner. Only a corner of the picture has the border on two sides that meet. Picking 'anywhere' means not using the border as a clue.

chart.title: Each piece cut in two: 2 rows of 4

flow.context: This is step 3 of the Cut-Up Picture, where a picture is cut into pieces and you put it together again. Here you put 8 pieces together, starting with the corners.

flow.do: 1. Your child shuts their eyes. 2. Take one piece away and mix the rest. 3. Your child puts the picture together and says what is on the missing piece. 4. Show the piece. Then keep all the pieces in the envelope.
flow.say: Shut your eyes. I am taking one piece away. Put the picture together. What is on the piece I am holding?
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. One piece is taken away. Put the picture together. What is on the missing piece?

ask.q: How did you know what was on the missing piece?
good: The cow's head is not there, so the missing piece must show the head.
I remembered the picture from before.
The pieces round the hole show what goes in it.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Cut-Up Picture, where a picture is cut into pieces and you put it together again. Here you work out what is on a missing piece.

activities.title: Maths in life: the Lid Puzzle
activities.context: In this activity you find the right lid for five boxes from the kitchen, and count how many tries you need. Then you put the boxes and lids in order of size and do it again. The point is to see how putting things in order saves tries.
activities.problem: Five boxes, five lids, all mixed up. How can you match them with the fewest tries?

materials.item: steel dabbas, tiffin boxes or bottles with lids, each a different size
one lid or cap that fits none of them
beans to count the tries, and a bowl

schedule.what: Match five mixed-up lids to five boxes and count the tries. Put boxes and lids in order of size and match again. Then find the lid that has no box.

activities.record: Write two numbers: the tries you needed with the lids mixed up, and the tries you needed with everything in order of size.

setup.art: Five round steel boxes of different sizes standing in a row on a kitchen floor, with their five lids in a mixed heap beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Take the lids off and mix them.

setup.art: A child trying a lid that is too small on a big steel box, with a bowl of beans beside her and one bean in her other hand.
setup.caption: 2. Try a lid. Drop a bean in the bowl for each try.

setup.art: The five boxes in a row from smallest to biggest, and the five lids in a row below them from smallest to biggest.
setup.caption: 3. Put boxes and lids in order of size. Match again.

flow.do: 1. Take the lids off the five boxes. 2. Mix the lids in a heap. Stand the boxes in a row, in any order. 3. Ask how many tries your child will need to put every lid on its box. Ask why. 4. Write the guess.
flow.say: Five boxes and five lids, all mixed up. How many tries will you need to match them all? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Five boxes, five lids. Guess how many tries you will need. Say why.

chart.title: One lid for each box

flow.context: This is the first step of the Lid Puzzle, where you find the right lid for every box in the kitchen. Here you mix up the lids and guess how many tries you will need.

flow.do: 1. Your child picks a lid and tries it on a box. 2. For every try, fit or no fit, your child drops one bean in the bowl. 3. Carry on until every box has its lid. 4. Count the beans together.
flow.say: Try a lid on a box. That is one try, so drop one bean in the bowl. Carry on until every box has its lid.
flow.kid: Try a lid on a box. Drop one bean for each try. Go on until every box has a lid.

ask.q: When a lid did not fit, what did you learn from that?
good: It was too small, so I tried a smaller box.
Not that box. One of the others.

flow.parent: Without a plan, five boxes can take up to 15 tries. Most children take between 7 and 12.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the Lid Puzzle, where you find the right lid for every box in the kitchen. Here you match the lids by trying, and count your tries.

flow.do: 1. Take the lids off again. Empty the bowl. 2. Your child stands the boxes in a row from smallest to biggest. 3. Your child lays the lids in a row from smallest to biggest. 4. Your child matches them again, with one bean for each try.
flow.say: This time, put the boxes in order from smallest to biggest. Do the same with the lids. Now match them. How many tries?
flow.kid: Put the boxes in order of size. Put the lids in order of size. Match them again. Count your tries.

ask.q: Why did you need fewer tries this time?
good: The smallest lid goes on the smallest box.
They were in the same order, so each lid fitted the first time.

flow.parent: With both rows in order, the tries come down to 5, one for each box. Ask your child to say why before you say anything.

check.q: A lid is too small for the middle box. Which boxes could it still fit?
check.why: Only smaller boxes. A lid that is too small for one box is also too small for every bigger box. So one try rules out several boxes at once.

chart.title: Tries with everything in order

flow.context: This is step 3 of the Lid Puzzle, where you find the right lid for every box in the kitchen. Here you put boxes and lids in order of size before matching.

flow.do: 1. Your child shuts their eyes. 2. Slip the extra lid in among the others and mix them. 3. Ask your child to find the lid that has no box. 4. Ask how they knew.
flow.say: Shut your eyes. I have added one lid that has no box. Find the odd lid. How do you know?
flow.kid: One lid has no box. Find the odd lid. Say how you know.

ask.q: How did you find the odd lid?
good: I matched all the others, and it was left over.
It was a different shape from every box.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Lid Puzzle, where you find the right lid for every box in the kitchen. Here you find the one lid that has no box.

activities.title: Everyone does maths: Ants and the Twig
activities.context: In this activity you find a line of ants, lay a twig across their way and watch what they do. The point is to see how other living beings solve a path puzzle. Do it only if you can find a line of ants at home or just outside.
activities.problem: A line of ants meets something new lying across their way. How do the ants find a way round?

materials.item: a line of ants, in the kitchen, on a balcony or on a wall outside
a twig, a pencil or a ruler
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Watch without touching the ants, because some ants bite. Lay the twig down gently, away from any ant. Take the twig away when you finish.

schedule.what: Watch a line of ants. Lay a twig across the line and watch for five to ten minutes. Draw the ants' way before and after.

activities.record: Draw two pictures: the ants' line before the twig, and the ants' way about ten minutes after the twig was put down.

setup.art: A child crouching near a wall, watching a thin line of small black ants walking along the edge of the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Find a line of ants. Watch them for two minutes.

setup.art: A pencil lying across the ants' line, with ants gathered on both sides and a few ants walking along the pencil's edge.
setup.caption: 2. Lay a twig or pencil across the line. Watch.

setup.art: The same pencil a few minutes later, with a new line of ants curving round one end of it.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the ants' new way.

flow.do: 1. Find a line of ants. 2. Sit a little way off and watch for two minutes. 3. Ask the three questions in the table. 4. Your child draws the ants' line on paper.
flow.say: Watch the ants without touching. Do they walk in one line? Do they go both ways? What do they do when two of them meet?
flow.kid: Watch the ants. Do not touch. Do they walk in one line? Draw the line.
flow.parent: Ants are easy to find near a kitchen shelf, a dustbin, a potted plant or the foot of a wall. If you cannot find any, watch the slime mould video in this lesson, which shows another living being in a maze.

chart.title: Look for these
rows: Do the ants walk in one line?
Do they touch when they meet?

flow.context: This is the first step of Ants and the Twig, where you watch how ants find a way round something laid across their line. Here you find a line of ants and watch them.

flow.do: 1. Ask what the ants will do if a twig lies across their line. Ask why. 2. Lay the twig gently across the line, not on any ant. 3. Watch for five to ten minutes. 4. Your child says aloud what the ants do: stop, turn back, go left, go right or climb over.
flow.say: What will the ants do when the twig is in their way? Why do you think so? Now watch. Tell me what you see.
flow.kid: Guess what the ants will do. Say why. Lay the twig across their line. Watch, and say what you see.

ask.q: Did all the ants do the same thing at first?
good: No. Some went left and some went right.
Some turned back.
Some climbed over.

flow.parent: At first the ants usually stop and spread out in several directions. After some minutes a new line forms. If the ants simply climb over the twig, that is a way through too. Try a wider thing, such as a ruler lying flat.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Ants and the Twig, where you watch how ants find a way round something laid across their line. Here you lay the twig down and watch what the ants do.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws the ants' new way. 2. Ask how the ants found it. Listen to your child's ideas. 3. Then read the parent note aloud. 4. Take the twig away.
flow.say: Draw the way the ants go now. How do you think they found it? Did one ant tell the others?
flow.kid: Draw the ants' new way. How do you think they found it?

ask.q: How do you think the ants found the new way?
good: Some ants tried different ways.
The others followed the ones who got through.
They can smell where other ants walked.

flow.parent: Read this after your child has given their ideas. Ants leave a smell on the ground as they walk, and other ants follow the smell. The ants who happen to find a short way round get across sooner, so that way gets more smell, and more ants follow. Scientists watched Argentine ants do this in 1989.

check.q: A twig blocks a line of ants. What do the ants usually do first?
options: They spread out and try different ways
They all wait for the twig to go
check.why: They spread out and try different ways. Some ways work and some do not. Soon most ants follow the way that worked. Picking 'they all turn left together' means thinking one ant gives orders to the rest.

chart.title: One family's notes (yours will be your own)
rows: a new line round one end

flow.context: This is the last step of Ants and the Twig, where you watch how ants find a way round something laid across their line. Here you draw the new way and talk about how the ants found it.

games.title: Odd One Out, Say Why
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a dice and card game. Four cards lie in a row, and the dice tells you which card you must make the odd one. You win a bean for a true reason. It builds quick thinking about what is the same and what is different.
rules: You need the 24 cards, a dice and a small heap of beans for scoring.
Mix the cards. Lay 4 cards face up in a row. Call the places 1, 2, 3 and 4.
On your turn, roll the dice. If you roll 1, 2, 3 or 4, you must make the card in that place the odd one.
Say your reason like this: 'It is the only one that…'. The reason must be true for that card and for no other card in the row.
If you roll 5, choose any card in the row. If you roll 6, swap all four cards for new ones and roll again.
The other players check the reason. A true reason wins one bean. If you find no reason by a slow count of ten, you win nothing.
A reason used once for a row may not be used again for that row. When every player has had a turn, lay 4 new cards.
The first player with 5 beans wins.
Playing alone: lay 4 cards and find a reason for each one. Can you get 4 out of 4, three rows running?

setup.art: Four small paper cards in a row on a floor mat showing a crow, a bus, a mango and the Moon, with a dice and a heap of beans beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay 4 cards in a row.

setup.art: A child who has rolled a 2 pointing at the second card, the bus, with a speech bubble that says 'It is the only one that…'.
setup.caption: 2. Roll. Make that card the odd one, with a reason.

setup.art: Another player nodding and handing over one bean.
setup.caption: 3. A true reason wins a bean.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 24 cards, or copy the words on slips of paper. Your child can draw each thing. 2. Mix the cards and lay 4 in a row. 3. Put the dice and a heap of beans nearby. 4. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: Four cards lie in a row. The dice will tell you which card to make the odd one. You must give a true reason.
flow.kid: Lay 4 cards in a row. The dice tells you which card must be the odd one.

chart.title: One row of four cards

flow.context: This is the first step of Odd One Out, Say Why, a dice and card game where you must find a true reason that makes one card the odd one. Here you set up.

flow.do: 1. Play one practice turn each. 2. Roll, point to the card and say the reason aloud. 3. Check together: is the reason true for this card and for no other?
flow.say: I rolled 3. The mango must be the odd one. It is the only one you can eat. Is that true of any other card?
flow.kid: Roll the dice. Point to that card. Say: it is the only one that…

check.q: The row is crow, bus, mango, Moon. You roll 2. Which reason makes the bus the odd one?
options: It is the only one with wheels
It is the only one you can see
It is the only one that moves
check.why: The bus is the only one with wheels. You can see all four, so that reason is true of every card. A crow moves too, and so does the Moon across the sky.

flow.parent: The most common slip is a reason that is true but also true of another card. Ask: 'Is that true of any other card in the row?'
flow.context: This is step 2 of Odd One Out, Say Why, a dice and card game where you must find a true reason that makes one card the odd one. Here you practise one turn.

flow.do: 1. Play the game. 2. Check every reason together. 3. When everyone has had a turn, lay 4 new cards.
flow.say: Your turn. Roll, and tell us why that card is the odd one. We will check your reason.
flow.kid: Play the game. Give a true reason to win a bean. Check the other players' reasons.

ask.q: Which card in this row was the hardest to make the odd one? Why?
good: The idli, because the dosa and the laddu are food too.
I had to look for something only that card has.

flow.context: This is step 3 of Odd One Out, Say Why, a dice and card game where you must find a true reason that makes one card the odd one. Here you play.

flow.do: 1. When a player has 5 beans, the game ends. 2. Ask which reason was the cleverest one of the game.
flow.say: Count your beans. Which reason did you like best today? Why?
flow.kid: The first player with 5 beans wins. Which reason did you like best?
flow.context: This is the last step of Odd One Out, Say Why, a dice and card game where you must find a true reason that makes one card the odd one. Here you finish and choose the best reason of the game.

games.title: Dice Switch
games.players: 2 to 4 players: with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a game with shape cards and a dice. One player lays a row of six cards. While the other player's eyes are shut, the dice decides which card is changed. The other player finds the change. It builds the skill of looking in order.

printables.title: 12 shape cards to draw and cut out

rules: Draw and colour the 12 shape cards on slips of paper. You also need a dice and beans for scoring.
One player is the maker. The maker lays 6 cards in a row and keeps the other 6 in a heap.
The finder looks at the row for a slow count of ten, then shuts their eyes.
The maker rolls the dice behind a hand. The number is the place to change. The maker swaps the card in that place for a card from the heap.
The finder opens their eyes and says which place changed.
The right place wins one bean. Saying what the old card was wins one more bean.
Swap jobs after every round. Play 6 rounds. The player with more beans wins.
A harder game: the maker rolls twice and changes two places. If both rolls are the same, only one place changes.

setup.art: Six small paper cards in a row on the floor, each with one coloured shape, and six more cards in a heap beside a dice.
setup.caption: 1. The maker lays a row of 6 shape cards.

setup.art: One child with both hands over her eyes while the other child rolls a dice behind a cupped hand.
setup.caption: 2. The finder shuts their eyes. The maker rolls.

setup.art: The first child pointing at the fourth card in the row while the other child nods.
setup.caption: 3. The finder says which place changed.

flow.do: 1. Draw the 12 shape cards on slips of paper and colour them. 2. Lay 6 cards in a row. Put the other 6 in a heap. 3. Count the places together from the left: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. 4. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: Here is a row of six cards. Let us count the places from the left. Soon one card will change. You must find which one.
flow.kid: Lay 6 shape cards in a row. Count the places from the left. One card will change.

chart.title: One row of six cards

flow.context: This is the first step of Dice Switch, a game where one card in a row is secretly changed and you find which one. Here you make the cards and lay the first row.

flow.do: 1. Play a practice round with your child as the finder. 2. Tell your child to say the row aloud in order before shutting their eyes. 3. Roll the dice behind your hand and swap that card. 4. Your child finds the change.
flow.say: Say the row aloud from left to right. Now shut your eyes. Open them. Which place has changed? What was there before?
flow.kid: Say the row aloud in order. Shut your eyes. Open them. Which place changed?

check.q: Look at the two rows. Which place changed?
check.why: Place 4. Check place by place from the left. Places 1, 2 and 3 match. At place 4 the red rectangle has become a yellow circle. Picking another place means looking at the whole row at once and guessing.

flow.parent: Saying the row aloud in order gives your child something to check against. Children who only glance at the row tend to guess.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Dice Switch, a game where one card in a row is secretly changed and you find which one. Here you play a practice round.

flow.do: 1. Play the game. Swap jobs after every round. 2. Lay a new row every two rounds. 3. Now and then, ask the finder how they found the change.
flow.say: Your turn to be the maker. Lay your row. I will shut my eyes. Roll the dice where I cannot see.
flow.kid: Take turns to be the maker. Roll the dice in secret. Change the card in that place.

ask.q: How did you find the change?
good: I said the row in my head and one card did not fit.
I checked each place from the left.
I remembered there was only one rectangle.

flow.context: This is step 3 of Dice Switch, a game where one card in a row is secretly changed and you find which one. Here you play.

flow.do: 1. After 6 rounds, count the beans. 2. Ask which change was the hardest to find, and why.
flow.say: Count your beans. Which change was the hardest to find? Why?
flow.kid: Count your beans. Which change was the hardest to find?
flow.context: This is the last step of Dice Switch, a game where one card in a row is secretly changed and you find which one. Here you finish and talk about the hardest change.

projects.title: Puzzle Post: five days, five puzzles
projects.context: In this five-day project you make one puzzle each day and post it to someone at home in an envelope. On the last day, everyone tells you their answers and their reasons, and you check them.
projects.problem: A puzzle is good only if someone else can solve it and say why. Can you make five that work?

materials.item: plain paper and squared paper from a maths notebook
crayons and a pencil
an old greeting card, and scissors for the grown-up
used envelopes, or paper folded into envelopes

projects.safety: A grown-up does the cutting on day 4.

schedule.what: Draw an odd one out puzzle: four things in a row. Whisper your own rule to a grown-up. Post it.
Draw a maze on squared paper, 5 squares by 5 squares, with one dead end. Post it.
Draw a row of 5 shapes. Draw it again below with one change. Post it.
A grown-up cuts an old card into 6 pieces. Post the pieces.
Collect the answers. For each puzzle, ask the solver for their reason and check it.

projects.record: Keep the five puzzles in their envelopes. On each envelope, write who solved it and one word about how.

setup.art: A child at a low table drawing four small things in a row on a slip of paper, with a few envelopes beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Make one puzzle each day.

setup.art: The child slipping a folded paper into an envelope with 'Thatha' written on it and leaving it on a pillow.
setup.caption: 2. Post it to someone at home.

setup.art: A grandfather holding up a solved paper maze while the child listens to him with her chin on her hands.
setup.caption: 3. On day 5, check each answer and its reason.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws four things in a row for an odd one out puzzle. 2. Your child whispers their rule to you. Write it on the back of your hand or on a hidden slip. 3. Your child puts the puzzle in an envelope and names who gets it. 4. Leave it where that person will find it.
flow.say: Draw four things. One must be the odd one. Whisper your rule to me. Then post your puzzle to someone at home.
flow.kid: Draw four things in a row. One is the odd one. Whisper your rule. Post the puzzle to someone.

chart.title: One idea for day 1

flow.context: This is day 1 of Puzzle Post, a five-day project where you make one puzzle each day for someone at home. Here you make and post an odd one out puzzle.

flow.do: 1. Day 2: your child draws a maze on squared paper, 5 squares by 5 squares, with one dead end. 2. Day 3: your child draws a row of 5 shapes, then the same row below with one change. 3. Day 4: you cut an old card into 6 pieces. 4. Each day, your child posts the puzzle to someone.
flow.say: A new puzzle today. Before you post it, solve it yourself once. Does it work?
flow.kid: Each day, make one new puzzle. Solve it yourself once. Then post it.

ask.q: How do you know your puzzle can be solved?
good: I tried it myself.
I walked my finger through the maze.
I counted, and only one shape is different.

flow.parent: Ask your child to solve each puzzle once before posting it. A maze with no way through, or a row with no change, is a common first slip.
flow.wait: Do one puzzle on each of the next three days.

chart.title: A day 2 maze can look like this

flow.context: These are days 2 to 4 of Puzzle Post, a five-day project where you make one puzzle each day for someone at home. Here you make a maze, a find-the-change puzzle and a cut-up card.

flow.do: 1. Your child visits each solver and asks for the answer. 2. Your child asks each solver: how do you know? 3. For the odd one out puzzle, your child says whether the solver's rule is the same as their own. 4. Ask whether a different rule can still be right.
flow.say: Ask each person for their answer and their reason. Is the reason true? Did anyone find a rule you had not thought of?
flow.kid: Ask each person for their answer. Ask: how do you know? Is the reason true?

ask.q: Someone picked a different odd one from yours. Is their answer wrong?
good: Not if their reason is true.
They used a different rule.
Mine was shape and theirs was colour.

chart.title: One family's post (yours will be your own)

flow.context: This is day 5 of Puzzle Post, a five-day project where you make one puzzle each day for someone at home. Here you collect the answers and check each reason.

challenges.title: Stretch: build a maze with only one way through
challenges.context: This is a design challenge that goes past Class 1. You draw a maze on a grid of 5 squares by 5 squares. It must have exactly one way from the ant to the banana, and at least two dead ends. The point is to find out how a maze maker thinks.
challenges.problem: Design a maze, 5 squares by 5 squares, with exactly one way from the ant to the banana and at least two dead ends.
constraints: The maze is 5 squares by 5 squares. The ant starts in the top left corner and the banana is in the bottom right corner.
There is exactly one way from the ant to the banana. Steps go up, down, left or right.
There are at least two dead ends.
materials: squared paper from a maths notebook, or plain paper ruled into a grid of 5 by 5 big squares
a dark crayon to shade the walls
a rajma to walk through the maze
general: Draw the true way first, in light pencil. Then add short side paths that stop.
Put a dead end at the very first fork.
Shade every square that is not on a path. Those squares are the walls.
creative: A dead end that runs towards the banana and stops one wall away from it.
A true way that first walks away from the banana.
One dead end with a fork of its own inside it.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own maze. Draw the true way first. Add two or more dead ends. Shade the walls. Then check that there is only one way through, and give the maze to someone to solve.

setup.art: A grid of five by five big squares drawn on paper, with a small ant drawn in the top left square and a banana in the bottom right square.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a grid of 5 by 5 squares. Mark the ant and the banana.

setup.art: The same grid with a light pencil line winding from the ant to the banana through the squares.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the true way first, in light pencil.

setup.art: The finished maze with the wall squares shaded dark, two short side paths ending in dead ends, and a rajma on the path.
setup.caption: 3. Add dead ends. Shade the walls. Test it.

flow.do: 1. Draw a grid of 5 by 5 squares, each about two fingers wide. 2. Read the problem and the three limits aloud. 3. Your child draws the ant and the banana in their corners. 4. Your child draws a winding way from the ant to the banana in light pencil.
flow.say: A maze maker draws the true way first. Draw a winding way from the ant to the banana. Do not go straight.
flow.kid: Draw the ant and the banana. Draw a winding way between them in light pencil.

chart.title: An empty grid: ant in one corner, banana in the other

flow.context: This is the first step of the maze-building challenge, where you design a maze with only one way through. Here you draw the grid and the true way.

flow.do: 1. Your child adds two side paths that branch off the true way and then stop. 2. Your child shades every square that is not on a path. 3. Count the dead ends together.
flow.say: Now add side paths that go nowhere. Where will a solver be most tempted to go wrong? Then shade all the wall squares.
flow.kid: Add two side paths that stop. Shade every square that is not a path. Count your dead ends.

ask.q: Where did you put your dead ends, and why there?
good: Near the start, so the solver must choose early.
Pointing towards the banana, so it looks like the right way.

flow.parent: Two side paths must not touch each other or touch the true way a second time. If they do, they make a second way through.

chart.title: An example: one way through and two dead ends

flow.context: This is step 2 of the maze-building challenge, where you design a maze with only one way through. Here you add the dead ends and shade the walls.

flow.do: 1. Your child walks a rajma through the maze and hunts for a second way to the banana. 2. If there are two ways, your child shades one more square to block one of them. 3. Check again.
flow.say: Is there only one way through? Hunt for a second way. If you find one, block it by shading one square.
flow.kid: Hunt for a second way to the banana. If you find one, shade a square to block it.

check.q: Your maze has two different ways to the banana. How do you leave only one?
options: Shade one square on one of the ways
check.why: Shade one square on one of the ways. That turns it into a dead end, and one way is left. Rubbing out a wall opens more paths, so it can add ways.

chart.title: This maze breaks the rule: it has two ways

flow.context: This is step 3 of the maze-building challenge, where you design a maze with only one way through. Here you check that your maze has only one way through.

flow.do: 1. Your child gives the maze to someone at home. 2. Your child counts slowly while the solver works. 3. Your child asks the solver which dead end fooled them. 4. Ask what your child would change to make the maze harder.
flow.say: Give your maze to someone. Count slowly while they solve it. Which dead end fooled them?
flow.kid: Give your maze to someone. Count while they solve it. Which dead end fooled them?

ask.q: What would you change to make your maze harder?
good: Make a dead end longer.
Put a dead end that points at the banana.
Make the true way turn away from the banana first.

flow.context: This is the last step of the maze-building challenge, where you design a maze with only one way through. Here you test your maze on a solver.

items.p: Which shape is the odd one out?
items.why: The triangle. The other three are circles. All four are red, so colour does not pick one out.

items.p: Which colour is the odd one here?
items.why: Yellow. Three squares are blue and one is yellow. All four are squares, so shape does not pick one out.

items.p: Which place holds the odd one? Write 1, 2, 3 or 4.
items.why: Place 1. It holds a triangle, and the other three places hold circles. All four are green.

items.p: Three spoons and one tumbler lie in a row. The tumbler is the odd one out.
items.why: True. Three things are spoons and one is not.

items.p: Sort each thing: does it have wheels or not?
items.why: The auto, the bus and the cycle roll on wheels. The boat, the crow and the banana have none. 'Has wheels' is a rule: it puts things in two groups.

items.p: How many dead ends does this maze have?
items.why: One. From the fork, the path going down stops after two squares. Every other white square leads on to the banana.

chart.title: Walk on the white squares

items.p: Which door leads the ant to the banana?
items.why: Door C. Start at the banana and walk backwards: up, left, left, then up to door C. Doors A and E each stop at a wall.

chart.title: Three doors: A, C and E

items.p: Count the steps on the ant's way to the banana. One step is one square.
items.why: 6 steps: right, down, right, down, down, right. There is only one way, with no fork.

chart.title: How many steps?

items.p: One shape changed from the top row to the bottom row. Which place?
items.why: Place 3. The triangle was yellow and is now red. Check place by place from the left, and stop where the rows do not match.

items.p: Match each thing to the group it belongs with.
items.why: A spoon is a kitchen thing. A crow is a bird. A mango is a fruit. A bus carries people on the road. Each group shares one rule.

items.p: Draw three things that are alike and one that is odd. Circle the odd one.
items.a: Any four things where three share something and the fourth does not, with the fourth circled.
items.why: A strong drawing lets a reader say the rule at once, for example three fruits and a shoe.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. In a maze, what do you do at a dead end?
items.a: I go back to the last fork and try a way I have not tried.
items.why: A strong answer says 'the last fork', not 'the start'. The squares before the last fork were fine.

items.p: Draw a row of 4 shapes. Draw it again below with one change. Ask someone to find the change.
items.a: Two rows of 4 shapes that match in three places and differ in one.
items.why: A strong puzzle has exactly one change. Check it yourself, place by place, before you show it.

items.p: The rule is colour. Which one is the odd one now?
items.why: The blue circle. Three shapes are red and one is blue. Picking the square means using the rule 'shape'.

items.p: This time the rule is shape. Which one is odd?
items.why: The square. Three shapes are circles and one is a square. Picking the blue circle means using the rule 'colour'.

items.p: One set of four things can have two different odd ones.
items.why: True. A different rule can pick out a different one. In the Odd One Out Test, each of the four cards was the odd one under some rule.

items.p: The ant can go two ways. How many steps is the shorter way?
items.why: 5 steps: down, down, down, right, right. The other way goes along the top and round. It takes 9 steps.

chart.title: Two ways to the banana

items.p: Which door should the ant take to reach the banana?
items.why: Door A. Start at the banana and walk backwards: left, left, left, then up to door A. Door C looks close, but it stops one wall above the banana.

chart.title: Which door?

items.p: You are stuck in a maze. Put the three steps in order.
items: Take a way you have not tried
Notice that the path has stopped
Go back to the last fork
a: Notice that the path has stopped
Go back to the last fork
Take a way you have not tried
items.why: First you notice the dead end. Then you go back to the last fork. Then you take a way you have not tried.

items.p: Is it a fork or a dead end?
items: The path splits into two ways
The path stops at a wall
You must choose left or right
items.why: At a fork you have a choice. At a dead end you have none, and you turn round.

items.p: How many shapes changed from the top row to the bottom row?
items.why: Two. At place 2 the blue circle became green. At place 5 the blue square became a blue triangle. The other three places match.

items.p: Banana, mango, lemon, carrot. Which is the odd one out?

views.says: The carrot. It is the only one that grows under the ground.
The lemon. It is the only sour one.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other child has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, then says what the other child has right.
items.why: Both reasons are true, so both answers are good. Each child chose a different rule: where the food grows, or how it tastes.

items.p: Draw four things so that each one can be the odd one. Tell a grown-up your four rules.
items.a: Four things, each with something that only it has. For example: a big red circle with a dot, a big red square, a big blue circle and a small red circle.
items.why: A strong set has one rule for each thing. Check each rule: is it true for that thing and for no other?

items.p: Three tumblers are exactly alike. The fourth thing is a plate. Can a tumbler be the odd one? Say why.
items.a: No. Anything true of one tumbler is true of the other two, so no rule picks out just one.
items.why: A strong answer says that the three tumblers are the same in every way. Only the plate has something the others lack.

items.p: A cut-up picture has a border. One piece has border on one side only. Where does it go?
opts: along an edge, not in a corner
items.why: Along an edge. A corner piece has border on two sides. A middle piece has none.

items.p: Match each set to the rule that three of them share.
items.why: Find what three of the four share. The fourth is the odd one: the cat, the spoon, the boat and the lamp.

items.p: How many of these four shapes can be the odd one, each with a true rule?
items.why: All 4. One is the only triangle. One is the only square. One is the only green shape. One is the only yellow shape.

items.p: Which rule makes the green circle the odd one?
opts: It is the only green one
It is the only one with corners
items.why: It is the only green one. It is not the only circle, because the yellow shape is a circle too. A circle has no corners.

items.p: This maze has two different ways to the banana.
items.why: True. One way goes straight down and then right, in 5 steps. The other goes along the top, down the right side and back, in 9 steps.

chart.title: One way or two?

items.p: Find every dead end in this big maze. How many are there?
items.why: Two. One is in the top right corner. The other is on the left side, near the bottom.

chart.title: The big maze

items.p: The ant is stuck at a dead end. Where is the best place to go back to?
items.why: The last fork. It is the nearest place that still has a way the ant has not tried.

items.p: Order these cut-up pictures from easiest to hardest to put together.
items.why: With more pieces, each piece has more places where it could go. So there is more to try and to rule out.

items.p: Does the puzzle have one answer only, or more than one good answer?
items: Which door leads to the banana?
Which is odd: crow, bus, mango, Moon?
How many steps is the shortest way?
Which of four friends is the odd one?
Which place changed in the row?
items.why: In a maze, a lid puzzle or a find-the-change puzzle, the answer is fixed and you find it. In an open odd one out, the answer depends on the rule you choose.

items.p: A cut-up picture has 4 pieces. You cut each piece in two. How many pieces now?
items.why: Each of the 4 pieces becomes 2 pieces. 2 and 2 and 2 and 2 make 8.

items.p: Keep one hand on the wall of a maze. Will you always get through?

views.says: Yes. The wall has to lead to the way out in the end.
Not always. If the banana is inside its own block of walls, you walk round and round.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other child has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, then says what the other child has right.
items.why: The second child is right about 'always'. The first child is right for mazes where every wall is joined to the outer wall. There the hand tip does work.

items.p: Draw a maze 5 squares by 5 squares, with one way through and two dead ends.
items.a: A grid of 5 by 5 squares with a start, an end, one way between them and two side paths that stop.
items.why: A strong maze has been tested by its maker: walk a finger through it and check that there is no second way.

items.p: Why is a wrong turn in a maze still useful?
items.a: It shows me one way that does not work. Now fewer ways are left to try.
items.why: A strong answer says that a dead end rules a way out. Each way you rule out brings you closer to the one that works.

items.p: Two shapes swapped places from the top row to the bottom row. Which two places?
items.why: Places 2 and 4. The blue triangle and the green circle have changed places. Places 1, 3 and 5 match.

items.p: Match each puzzle to a good first move.
pairs: start at the end and walk backwards
find what three of them share
check place by place from the left
items.why: Each kind of puzzle has a way in. A good first move makes the puzzle smaller before you start trying things.

quiz.p: Which one does not belong with the others?
quiz.why: The circle. The other three are squares. All four are green, so colour does not pick one out.

quiz.p: Idli, dosa, vada, tumbler. Which is the odd one, and why?
opts: the tumbler: it is not food
quiz.why: The tumbler, because the other three are food. 'The idli: it is food' fails, because the dosa and the vada are food too.

quiz.p: Someone picks the red circle as the odd one. Which rule are they using?
quiz.why: Colour. The red circle is the only shape that is not blue. By shape, the triangle would be the odd one.

quiz.p: With the same four things, a new rule can make a different one the odd one.
quiz.why: True. Red circle, red square, blue circle: by shape the square is odd, and by colour the blue circle is odd.

quiz.p: The ant may go in at A, C or E. Which door leads to the banana?
quiz.why: Door E. Start at the banana and walk backwards: right, then up to door E. Door C goes a long way down and then stops at a wall.

chart.title: Which door?

quiz.p: Count the dead ends in this maze.
quiz.why: Three. One is in the top row, one square past the first fork. One is in the top right corner. One is in the bottom left corner.

chart.title: Walk on the white squares

quiz.p: You reach a dead end in a maze. What is the best thing to do?
opts: Go back to the last fork
quiz.why: Go back to the last fork and take a way you have not tried. Starting again makes you walk over squares that were fine.

quiz.p: A maze has three doors and one end. What is a quick way to find the right door?
opts: Start at the end and walk backwards
Pick the door nearest the end

quiz.p: An odd one out answer is good only if its reason is true.
quiz.why: True. 'The square is odd because it is blue' is a wrong answer if the square is red. The reason is part of the answer.

quiz.p: A friend picks a different odd one from you and gives a true reason. What does that mean?
quiz.why: Both answers can be right. Your friend used a different rule. Each answer is right for its own rule.

applications: A doctor looks for the one sign in your body that is not as usual, and asks why.
A mechanic listens to an engine for the one sound that does not fit.
A farmer sorting mangoes picks out the few that are not like the rest, before they spoil the others.
An electrician hunting for a fault checks one switch at a time and rules out the ones that work.
A delivery rider in an old town goes back to the last turning when a lane is closed, and tries the next lane.
A tailor fits cut pieces of cloth together, like a cut-up picture, so that the design matches at the seams.
People who write computer programs tell a computer how to find the way across a map, one fork at a time.
Astronomers still find new things in the sky by spotting the one light that does not behave like the rest.

open_questions.q: How does a slime mould find the short way, with no brain that anyone has found?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that the tubes in a slime mould's body grow wider where more liquid flows and shrink where little flows. They are still working out how this adds up to such good choices.

open_questions.q: Is every puzzle that is quick to check also quick to solve?
open_questions.why_open: Checking a finished number puzzle is quick. Solving a big one can take very long. Nobody has proved whether a quick way to solve must exist whenever a quick way to check exists. A prize of one million dollars waits for the proof.

open_questions.q: Do bees mean by 'same' what we mean by 'same'?
open_questions.why_open: Bees pass the tests that scientists set. But nobody can look out through a bee's eyes, so scientists still argue about what the bees are doing.

open_questions.q: Why do people enjoy puzzles, even with no prize?
open_questions.why_open: Children all over the world play with puzzles for no reward. Scientists have several ideas about why working things out feels good, and no agreed answer.

maths.problem: In one maze, the long way to the banana is 9 steps. The short way is 5 steps. How many steps does the short way save?
maths.explain: Take the short way from the long way. 9 take away 5 leaves 4. So the short way saves 4 steps.
maths.context: In Ant and Banana you walked an ant through mazes. One maze in this lesson has two ways to the banana. This problem compares them.
maths.why_maths: Counting the steps of each way and taking one from the other tells you which way is shorter, and by how much, without guessing.

maths.problem: A cut-up picture has 4 pieces. A grown-up cuts each piece in two. How many pieces are there now?
maths.explain: Each of the 4 pieces becomes 2. That is double 4. 4 and 4 make 8.
maths.context: In the Cut-Up Picture a card was cut into 4 pieces, and then each piece was cut in two. This problem counts the pieces.
maths.why_maths: Knowing the double tells you how many pieces to look for, so that you notice if one has slipped under the mat.

maths.problem: In Dice Switch the row has 6 cards. You have checked places 1 to 4, and they have not changed. In how many places can the change still be?
maths.explain: There are 6 places. You have ruled out 4. 6 take away 4 leaves 2. The change is in place 5 or place 6.
maths.context: In the game Dice Switch one card in a row of six is changed in secret. This problem is about what you know after checking part of the row.
maths.why_maths: Taking away the places you have ruled out shows how small the puzzle has become. With 2 places left, one more look settles it.

chart.title: Places 1 to 6. Places 1 to 4 are checked.

maths.problem: In one family's Odd One Out Test, 3 people picked the square and 2 people picked the blue circle. How many more people picked the square?
maths.explain: Match each square pick with a blue circle pick. Two pairs are made, and one square pick is left over. So 1 more person picked the square.
maths.context: In the Odd One Out Test you asked people at home to pick the odd card. This problem compares the picks in one family.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two counts shows which card most people see as odd first. It does not show which answer is right, because both had true reasons.

maths.problem: There are 5 boxes and 5 lids. You have matched 3 boxes. You pick up the 4th box. How many lids are left to try on it?
maths.explain: 5 lids take away the 3 already used leaves 2. If the first of them does not fit, the other one must. So one try is enough to know.
maths.context: In the Lid Puzzle you matched five lids to five boxes. This problem is about the moment when most of the lids are already on.
maths.why_maths: Taking away the lids already used shows how few are left. The puzzle gets easier with every lid you place.

playtest: Walked through every flow as a parent and one child in a flat. Every maze in the lesson was checked by a small program: each has the number of ways, dead ends and steps that the text says. The four test cards were checked too: the dot, the square, the blue colour and the small size each belong to one card only. The Odd One Out Test works with two people, and is better with three or four. If everyone picks the same card at first, the hunt for a rule for each card still gives the result. Copying the big maze on paper takes a grown-up about three minutes. The Lid Puzzle needs five boxes of clearly different sizes. With two boxes of nearly the same size, the tries in order go above 5. Ants and the Twig depends on finding ants, so it is outside the core path. The ants may take longer than ten minutes, or may climb over a thin twig. Dice Switch needs 12 hand-drawn cards, about five minutes of drawing. Step minutes add up to each part's minutes. Looked up on the web while writing: the slime mould maze paper of 2000, the honeybee paper of 2001, the Argentine ant paper of 1989 (title and summary only, not the full papers), Lucas's 1882 chapter on Trémaux's rule (read in English translation), the hand-on-wall rule and where it fails, the labyrinth on coins from Crete, the chakravyuha carving at Halebidu, the Greek word behind 'planet', Udana 6.4 and Thirukkural 423. Not looked up, written from memory: Euler and the seven bridges in 1736, the one-million-dollar prize for the checking and solving question, how a slime mould's tubes widen and shrink, the yellow colour of the slime mould, and the book by Christopher Danielson. Mazes of hedges being hundreds of years old is from general knowledge. The three videos were confirmed by title and channel only, not watched, so watch each one before showing it. The mazes are drawn as tables of black and white squares with an ant and a banana symbol, because there is no maze chart yet. How they look should be checked on a phone.
